summary:
Blinkscope is a web-based blink comparator for NASA's SPHEREx mission. Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930 by flipping between two photographs of the same sky and watching for a dot that jumped. Blinkscope does the same with SPHEREx, which images the whole sky in 102 infrared colours about every six months.

Enter any sky position or object name. The tool finds every public SPHEREx exposure covering that spot, aligns them north-up, and plays them in sequence so anything that moves or changes stands out. Users can switch between six detectors, build colour plates, subtract the first image, overlay Gaia and WISE catalogue sources, plot a light curve, stack exposures along a suspected motion, export a GIF, and report a candidate. Everything runs in the browser, reading pixels directly from NASA's public archive, with no install or account.

This addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by making the search for distant, slow-moving objects such as a possible ninth planet or nearby brown dwarfs open to anyone. More than 100 TB of survey data is public, but few people can easily look at it. Five known moving or variable stars and brown dwarfs are included as test targets, so users can see what a real detection looks like before searching on their own.
details:
What it does

Blinkscope is a blink comparator for SPHEREx that runs in a web browser. You give it a sky position or an object name. It finds every public SPHEREx exposure of that spot, lines them up with north at the top, and plays them one after another. Anything that moves or changes brightness between visits stands out to the eye, the same way Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto on photographic plates in 1930.

How it works

1. The site asks NASA's IRSA archive which SPHEREx images cover the position.

2. The browser reads only the small strip of each image it needs, straight from NASA's public cloud storage. Each file is about 65 MB, so this avoids downloading gigabytes.

3. Each strip is resampled onto a shared north-up grid, the sky background is removed, and exposures are stacked per survey pass, about six months apart.

4. The stacked plates are played as a blink.

Tools in the viewer

- Six detectors covering 0.75 to 5.0 microns, and colour plates built from three of them

- Subtract the first plate, so only what changed remains

- Gaia and WISE catalogue overlays, to tell known stars from unknowns

- A light curve, and a measurement across all 102 SPHEREx bands

- Shift-and-stack along a suspected motion, to bring out faint movers

- GIF export, shareable links, an embeddable view, and a candidate report form

The rest of the site

- A full-sky map of the real sky with constellations and the Milky Way, where you can click any spot to blink it, and see where SPHEREx is right now

- Five worked examples: three that move (Barnard's Star, the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B) and two that change brightness (RW Aurigae, R Draconis)

- A 3D film of the launch and a pull-apart model of the observatory

- A Method page that states the limits of the approach

Benefits and intended impact

More than 100 TB of SPHEREx data is public, but looking at it normally takes astronomy software and programming. Blinkscope needs no install, no account and no code. The aim is to let students, amateur astronomers and curious people join the search for distant, slow-moving objects such as a possible ninth planet or nearby brown dwarfs, and to give them a way to report what they find. New SPHEREx images appear in the tool on their own as NASA releases them.

How it is creative

It brings a 100-year-old discovery method to a telescope launched in 2025. The site treats the data as plates on a light table, and the opening retells the real launch of 11 March 2025 in 3D, with the mission clock matched to the actual flight. The worked examples teach what a real detection looks like before you search on your own.

What we considered

- Honesty about limits: a SPHEREx pixel is about 6 arcseconds across, so only fast or nearby objects move visibly. The Method page says so.

- Speed: plates for the five examples are pre-rendered so they load at once.

- Accessibility: keyboard controls throughout, and the opening animation is skipped for people who ask for reduced motion.

- Reliability: the archive is sometimes slow or busy, so the tool retries and explains the wait.

Tools and data

- Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, Next.js, React

- Graphics and motion: Three.js (WebGL), GSAP, Lenis

- Testing: Vitest, Playwright, axe-core

- Hosting: Vercel

- Custom code to read FITS astronomy files and their sky coordinates in the browser

- Data: SPHEREx images (NASA/IRSA, hosted on AWS Open Data), Gaia DR3, AllWISE, SIMBAD/Sesame, Yale Bright Star Catalogue, NASA SVS Deep Star Maps, d3-celestial constellation data

- AI assistance: Claude Code (Anthropic) was used during development
